![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227209/assets/643d8218715b65def0d9fd274c50b18c76cfbea35cd3dc70f3cdbb5c5b16b6f8.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$2,$ as shown above. What is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =4+l+\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $4,$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<4.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ l & =\sqrt{16-{l}^{2}} \\ {l}^{2} & =16-{l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =16 \\ {l}^{2} & =8 \\ l & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=2\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,2\sqrt{2})$ | $2\sqrt{2}$ | $(2\sqrt{2},4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $3$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=2\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\sqrt{2}) & =4+2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{16-(2\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =4+2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{16-8} \\  & =4+2\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{2} \\  & =4+4\sqrt{2} \\  & =4(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
